reason: On bracts, scales, stipules and glume-like parts, chaffy means thin, dry and membranous, which is FLOPO scarious. 'Receptacle chaffy' means paleae are present, which is flower bract (PO_0009034, synonym chaff) present, so the receptacle must be excluded and given its own rule.

Corrugated seeds, fruits, bark and blades have a surface thrown into many wrinkles or folds, which is PATO:0001359 rugose. The accepted rule R0066 already maps 'corrugate' to rugose; plicate and furrowed are narrower or different.

PATO:0104355 ascending is 'directed gradually upward at an oblique angle', which is what a curved-ascending stem or pedicel does. The curve is part of the botanical sense of ascending, not a second value.

Reclining is ambiguous in floras: leaning on a support (semi-scandent), lying down, or bent backwards. It is not reliably decumbent (lying on the ground with rising tips). PATO:0001965 reclinate is a curled quality and does not fit either.
FLOPO umbelliform is defined only for inflorescences with flowers arising from about one point. An umbrella-shaped crown, stigma or fruit is a different, flat-topped spreading shape.

'Polymorphic' is mostly said of species or populations (a taxonomic remark), or of variation in colour, hairiness or size, not only shape. Mapping it to PATO variant shape on the bearer would make false phenotypes. The dimorphic and heterophylly cases need their own terms.
Baccate means berry-like, so fleshy is right for fruits and for fleshy cones or seeds (Juniperus, Taxus). On other parts the word does not occur in that sense.

FLOPO included means not projecting beyond the structure that encloses it, and it is not limited to stamens and styles. Its bearer list already includes fruit, sepal and ovary parts. 'Stamens enclosed', 'nut enclosed in the cupule' and 'fruit enclosed by the accrescent calyx' are all this quality. The enclosing part is missing in both words alike.

A metallic sheen or lustre is a kind of high reflectivity, so it falls under PATO:0001373 glistening. The metal-like detail is lost, but the parent is correct, as with arcuate to curved. A colour word with it ('metallic blue') is mapped separately. Iridescent needs a colour change with viewing angle.

Paleaceous of pappus elements, bracts and scales means chaffy, which is scarious. 'Receptacle paleaceous' (Asteraceae) means the receptacle bears paleae, which is flower bract (PO_0009034) present, so the receptacle must be excluded.

A flange is a thin, flattened rim projecting from the body (spore equator, fruit, stipule margin). That fits PATO:0104354 winged ('thin, flattened extensions that project from its main body'). A flange is a narrow wing, not a different quality.

PO:0025349 awn is defined as an appendage of a glume, lemma or palea. A bristle-tipped leaf, tooth or phyllary has a bristle point, which is better covered by FLOPO hair-pointed (FLOPO:0991249) or mucronate (FLOPO:0991054), not by awn present.

'Radial' is ambiguous: radial symmetry of flowers, radial walls and sections, radially arranged ribs or rays. Radiating fits only the last. The flower sense already has R0607 (radially symmetric to actinomorphic); a flower-only rule for 'radial' to PATO:0001328 actinomorphic can be added separately.
On stems and axes, pithy means containing pith (PO:0006109). On fruit it means spongy flesh, which is not pith.

'Flowers panicled' or 'inflorescence panicled' says the flowers are borne in a panicle, so panicle inflorescence (PO:0030123) present is the right reading. This matches how 'aristate' is mapped to awn present (C207). When the adjective qualifies another named inflorescence type, FLOPO panicle-like (FLOPO:0991198) is the alternative.

In floras, 'knobbed' styles, stigmas, hairs and connectives end in a knob, which is the FLOPO head-shaped definition ('abruptly enlarged at its tip into a rounded head'). A surface bearing many knobs is 'knobby/knobbly' (PATO:0002427 knobbled), a different word.
FLOPO crisped is a margin quality, and 'crisp' means crisped on leaf and perianth parts. On fruits, stems and other parts 'crisp' means a brittle texture, and on hairs it means curly.

The rule is already limited to plant, stem and habit. In the tropical floras (French 'sarmenteux'), a sarmentose shrub is a scrambling, half-climbing one. FLOPO climbing is defined to include leaning on a support. The runner (stolon) sense is rare in these descriptions.

Well-defined usually means sharply delimited or distinct from the neighbouring part (well-defined petiole, keel, border), not clearly visible. There is no PATO or FLOPO term for 'distinct', and PATO:0005006 differentiated from needs the second part.
Glands, stomata and sori that are embedded in the surface are below its level, which is PATO:0002416 sunken. 'Seeds embedded in pulp' describes containment, and sunken would be wrong there.

'Veins invisible' or 'nerves invisible beneath' is the extreme of not being clearly visible, which falls under PATO:0000464 inconspicuous. It does not say the part is absent, so the broader correct term is the safe mapping.
Gland-like means resembling a gland (gland-like teeth, appendages), not bearing glands or being glandular tissue. Mapping it to PATO:0002117 glandular would claim glands are present.

Veiny means conspicuously veined, which is a visibility statement, not presence. The target PO:0005020 is the vascular bundle, not leaf lamina vein (PO:0020138). The right form is vein + conspicuous (a pattern with a part), not a single-word rule.
'Level' is vague (flat, even, 'at the level of', 'level with' X). PATO flush needs a second surface, which the word alone does not give.
Laminate means either having a blade or layered (bark, testa). It does not reliably mean that a lamina is present.
A tetrahedron is a triangular pyramid, so tetrahedral is a narrower case of PATO:0002336 pyramidal. Mapping to the broader correct class is acceptable, as with arcuate to curved.
Poorly defined margins, zones or veins are indistinctly delimited, which is not the same as low visibility. There is no 'indistinct' term. This matches the drop of 'well-defined' (R0160).
An obtusely pointed apex narrows to a blunt point, which is the same reading as 'blunt-pointed', already mapped to PATO obtuse (R1816). It is not subacute (nearly acute).
Stigmatic means 'of the stigma' (stigmatic surface, lobes, branches). It names part of the stigma, so it belongs with the bearer, and it does not state that a stigma is present.

Bicolorous means a part has two colours (for example petals white with a pink base). PATO multi-colored (synonym variegated) is the correct broader term. FLOPO discolorous is about compared surfaces, typically the two leaf faces, differing in colour.
